Four are behaviour-only and snapshot-covered: `tiddlywiki5.blockquote`, `tiddlywiki5.macro-string-params`, `tiddlywiki5.mvv-display`, `tiddlywiki5.pragma-params-mvv` (127 assertion lines between them).** I concede those four as fusible into snapshot coverage. The fifth candidate, `macro-dynamic-params`, I **defend**, on the measured absence of six of its seven constructs from every sample. **The general finding for the consolidating reader: scope-vocabulary subsumption is not a safe collapse criterion for this suite.** Two independent properties defeat it — negation (unrepresentable in the snapshot format) and construct presence (vocabulary can be covered while the construct is absent). Any fixture collapse must test both. ### A2. The colour cluster: the load-bearing claim CONFIRMED, the exact integers not reproducible I re-ran the two derivations that decide whether the cluster is one instrument or several. **(i) `construct-legibility`'s container claim. CONFIRMED, and strengthened.** Its header asserts that no theme rule reaches the container scopes of a call or a transclusion, so a reading taken on containers alone collapses four distinct constructs into one ink — *"A gate built on containers would have ruled a healthy grammar broken."* I loaded all 65 bundled themes through the repository's own single theme resolver and asked directly: | selector root | themes with any rule reaching it | |---|---| | `meta.variable.call` | **0 of 65** | | `meta.transclusion` | **0 of 65** | | `meta.variable` | 2 of 65 | | `meta` | 65 of 65 | Resolving the container stacks of a call, a filter run, a transclusion and prose, I get **all four identical in 65 of 65 themes** — against the header's stated 44 of 65. My reading is stricter than the tool's (the tool builds its stacks by tokenizing real specimens, so its container stacks carry whatever ancestors the grammar actually emits; mine are constructed). **The claim's substance holds in both readings, and mine is the harsher one: the container reading is worthless as a basis for a legibility gate.** The distinction between those four constructs rides entirely on the punctuation and name scopes inside them. **`construct-legibility` must not be fused into any container-grain or scope-name-grain colour reader.** **(ii) `contrast-witness`'s quiet-rule derivation. CONFIRMED in rank and ratio.** Its header asserts that about one foreground rule in ten across the 65 themes sets the colour the editor already had, and that `variable` is the single worst-shipped such selector — which is why every `variable.*` name in the grammar reads as ordinary prose to a large minority of readers. My independent re-derivation: **1,467 quiet of 15,116 foreground rule-parts = 9.7%** (header: 1,191 of 11,756 = 10.1% — different denominator, same ratio). And ranking selectors by how many ruling themes leave the colour unchanged, **`variable` comes first: quiet in 23 of the 59 themes that rule on it = 39%** (header: 18 of 54 = 33%). Runners-up I measured: `variable.other` 23/43, `string` 18/62, `meta.embedded` 17/23, `markup.bold` 11/55, `markup.italic` 11/46. **I report a false start honestly:** my first run keyed its per-theme sets on a theme-name field that is undefined for most of these files, collapsing all 65 themes into one and reporting "`variable`: ruled on by 1 theme." That was a broken probe, not a refutation. Re-keyed on file index, it reproduces. **(iii) The shared provenance anecdote (YIN's D3).** `theme-parity`, `dark-construct` and `contrast-witness` all narrate the same origin story — a heading coloured in 9 of 65 themes while every gate read green. That event predates the vocabulary work in this release, so it **cannot be re-run against today's grammar**, and I did not try. YIN is right that it is one anecdote in three places. **It is not evidence of one instrument**: the three mechanisms are distinct and I verified the distinction structurally — absent rule (`dark-construct`), rule present but within CIE76 ΔE of the theme default (`contrast-witness`), rule present but below the median of six comparator markup grammars (`theme-parity`). **CONDITIONAL: the anecdote should live in one place; the three gates stay.** **A finding that falls out of (i) and (ii) and belongs to both our reports.** Neither derivation reproduces the header's *exact* integers from the shipped modules — 65 vs 44, 1467/15116 vs 1191/11756, 23/59 vs 18/54. Every one reproduces the rank, the direction and the ratio. **So the harness's own doc-comment integers are dated readings presented in the present tense, exactly like the record's figures, and nothing welds either.** This is the same defect as YIN's R2 and my own §3.3 from wave one, and it is one defect, not two. See PART C. ### A3. D4, the six readings of `/^OWED/`: LATENT, and sharper than YIN stated **Verified, with exact sites.** Six code sites test whether a ledger row's reason opens with `OWED`. Three strip a `READER ` prefix first by calling the shared `readerOf()` reader; three do not: | site | strips `READER ` first? | ledger it reads | |---|---|---| | `ablation-witness.js:361` | **yes** (`readerOf(...).rest`) | `ablation-ledger.txt` | | `darkness-witness.js:219` | **yes** | `darkness-ledger.txt` | | `swallow-witness.js:107-108` | **yes** | `swallow-ledger.txt` | | `light-cone.js:81` | **NO** (tests the raw reason) | **`swallow-ledger.txt`** | | `bracket-witness.js:155` | **NO** (tests the raw reason) | `bracket-ledger.txt` | | `delimiter-inheritance.test.js:96,106` | **NO** (`/#\s*OWED/i` on the raw line) | `delimiter-ledger.txt` | Neither `light-cone.js` nor `bracket-witness.js` imports the reader-scope module at all. **The divergence is sharper than YIN described: `light-cone.js` and `swallow-witness.js` read THE SAME FILE** — `corpus/swallow-ledger.txt`. So this is not "the day a row lands in one of two files"; it is one file read by two gates with two incompatible predicates. No second file is needed. **It is latent, and I can say exactly how latent.** `READER OWED` rows that exist today, by file: | ledger | `READER OWED` rows | bare `OWED` rows | any `READER` tag | |---|---|---|---| | `darkness-ledger.txt` | **65** | 28 | 84 | | `ablation-ledger.txt` | **7** | 323 | 37 | | `expected-divergence.txt` | **4** | 9 | 22 | | `swallow-ledger.txt` | **0** | 0 | **5** | | `bracket-ledger.txt` | 0 | 4 | 0 | | `delimiter-ledger.txt` | 0 | 1 | 0 | **This corrects YIN's distribution.** The total is 76 as YIN said, but they are **not** all in `darkness-ledger`: 65 there, 7 in `ablation-ledger`, 4 in `expected-divergence`. All three of those files are read by stripping readers, so all 76 are handled correctly today. The two non-stripping readers happen to read the three files that carry none. **What would make it live: one row.** `swallow-ledger.txt` already carries **five** `READER ` rows (four scoped `READER 5.4.1`, one `READER 5.5.0-prerelease`, naming unterminated-run recovery differences between the pinned release and the operator's fork). **Adding `OWED` to any one of those five, or writing a sixth `READER OWED` row, makes it live immediately.** **And the consequence is worse than "they disagree."** `light-cone`'s gate rule is one-sided by design: it refuses only when a row is filed as *owed* and an arm proves the deciding evidence sits outside the grammar's reach. A row filed `READER 5.4.1 OWED` reads to `light-cone` as *ruled*, which moves it out of the refusable set into the merely-reported set. **The gate cannot go red on that row at all.** It does not disagree loudly; it goes silent. That is precisely the failure mode the whole harness is built to refuse. **Cost to fix: one shared `owedOf()` beside the existing `readerOf()`, and three call-site edits.** This is YIN's ranked item 3 and I rank it **first** — above every dead-code deletion. It is the only item on either list where a latent fault silently disarms a gate. ### A4. D8, the ward's blind spot: lifting the exclusion is UNSAFE, and the file says why **The exclusion is narrower than YIN described.** `one-implementation.test.js` builds two populations: `all` (every `.js` under the tools tree, tests included) and `sources` (line 31, `all` minus `*.test.js`). Only the **fingerprint scan** — the check that two files do the same work — uses `sources`. Four other checks in the same file use `all` and so already reach into tests: the TiddlyWiki-resolution check, the subprocess-spawn check, the grammar-field-reading check, and one check that explicitly selects `.test.js` files. That last group carries a **named exemption map of five `.test.js` files** allowed to read a grammar field directly. **And the exclusion carries its reason in the two lines above it:** *"A test sits beside the instrument it collides, and naming the work marks how it collides — `theme-paint.test.js` reads a theme on purpose, to prove the tool reads it the same way. Holding a test to the rule would forbid the collision that proves the rule."* **That is a real tension, not an oversight.** Two house requirements pull against each other: one invariant forbids a test from holding a *second implementation* of a reading (because the two drift in silence — it records a case where a colour relation read green in a test file and refused in the tool, and the duplicate passed for as long as it disagreed); while the collider requirement demands a test that *constructs faulty input directly*, which often means doing the computation in the test. The `.test.js` exclusion on the fingerprint scan is where that tension is resolved. **Lifting it wholesale would make the house's own required collisions into violations.** **RULING: CONDITIONAL. The exclusion stays; extend the existing named-exemption mechanism to the fingerprint scan instead.** The mechanism already exists in the same file (the five-entry map). **What lifting it would newly surface — measured, and one of YIN's two items is not a duplication:** - **A byte-identical `scopesOn` helper in exactly two invariants.** `image-attribute-list.test.js:33` and `attribute-value-across-lines.test.js:33` carry the same 12-line function — same signature `(source, word)`, same body, same space-joined-string return. **Genuine duplication. YIN's count of two is right.** - **I was wrong to say three.** A third invariant, `pragma-zone.test.js:31`, carries a function *of the same name* that is a **different function**: signature `(source, part)`, offset-based rather than text-matching, asserts the probe actually contains the part, and returns an **array** rather than a joined string. A fingerprint scan keyed on the work would not flag it. **But three files sharing one name across two return types is a legibility hazard nothing reads** — my addition to the list. - **`source ./grammars.sh` inlined once, not twice.** `memetic-containment.test.js:37` carries the same `bash -c 'source ./grammars.sh …; printf "%s\n" "${ARGS[@]}"'` incantation that the shared tokenizer module holds at its line 32. **Genuine duplication.** The second file YIN named, `vendored-grammars.test.js`, *reads* `grammars.sh` as a file to hold its named paths against the tree — a different act, correctly not a duplication. So lifting the exclusion would newly surface **two** real duplications, not three or four — and would simultaneously flag an unknown number of deliberate collisions. **The two duplications can be fixed directly, today, without touching the ward.** That is the cheap half of YIN's item 4, and I endorse it unreservedly; the ward half I decline. ### A5. The debt backlogs: I CONCEDE, with one condition that is not negotiable This is the item where the evidence went against my pole, and it goes decisively. **My sample: not a sample. I read every OWED reason in both files programmatically** — all 359 rows of the ablation ledger and all 111 of the darkness ledger — stripped the `OWED` / `READER OWED` prefix from each, and counted distinct reason bodies. | | rows | OWED rows | **distinct OWED reason bodies** | distinct 60-char stems | |---|---|---|---|---| | `ablation-ledger.txt` | 359 | 319 | **22** | 22 | | `darkness-ledger.txt` | 111 | 92 | **5** | 3 | Distinct bodies equals distinct stems in the ablation ledger, which means **there is no variation inside a family at all** — the reasons are byte-identical repeats. The largest families: - ablation: **96 rows** carrying one identical sentence about a style run's `;`/`:` separators splitting declarations into the built element's style attribute; then 40 (tag-name pattern), 38 (a `.` opening a heading/list/quote leader), 38 (two-or-more hyphens building a dash), 23, 18, 14, 10. - darkness: **89 rows** carrying one identical sentence about a filter or template-title value genuinely spanning a blank line; then 2, then 1. **Zero rows in either file carry a reason that is only a back-reference** ("the same reading…"), so this is not abbreviation — it is full verbatim duplication, 96 and 89 times. And the darkness ledger states its 89-row cause **a second time, in its own header comment** at lines 60-62. The cause already has a single home. **RULING: these are not 319 and 92 guards. They are 22 and 5 causes, enumerated at a row granularity the key grammar forces.** The ablation ledger's row key is ` ` — one row per *character position*. So 96 identical sentences is what one cause looks like when it touches 96 characters. YIN is substantively right: as *reasons*, these two files have become records. **THE CONDITION, and it is structural rather than stylistic.** A single ruling cannot simply absorb 96 sites today, because the house guards exactly that move. A separate single-number ratchet file is **seated at 1** and reads: *"How many CAUSES the widest ruling in any ledger can absorb. The count may fall and may never rise… every ruling in every ledger names exactly one cause."* Its own header records why it exists: a predecessor ratchet measuring the *share of corpus tokens* under some ruling re-seated four times in one session (55.8% → 56.6% → 57.2% → 60.0%), every reason true, because the corpus is authored and writing more of what is already ruled raises the share without widening any key. The stopping condition for the whole healing effort can be met by **ruling generously**, and that ratchet is the only thing refusing it. A wildcarded key spanning 96 character positions is exactly the move that ratchet refuses — unless the row granularity and the cause granularity are separated. **So: CONDITIONAL. The two largest corpus files can collapse from 319 + 92 OWED rows to 22 + 5 rulings once — and only once — the ledger row grammar carries a `cause` identifier distinct from its `key`, with the breadth ratchet re-seated to count distinct causes per ruling rather than distinct keys.** Without that, the row count is the price of the only guard against the harness congratulating itself. With it, the collapse removes roughly 400 lines of verbatim repetition from the two largest ledgers and loses nothing — and it is the single largest honest reduction on either of our lists. --- ## PART B — DEFEND / CONCEDE ON YIN'S CANDIDATES ### B1. `snap-tid` + `snap-meta` — **CONCEDE** Two gates, one instrument, one scope (`source.tiddlywiki5.tid-file`), two globs over **2** and **1** sample files respectively. Fusing to one glob compares the same three snapshots. The only thing the split buys is a separate verdict line and separate exercise of the manifest's `.meta` → `tid` file association — and a different invariant already holds the file associations, independently, by reading the manifest. I called this the weakest-defended gate in wave one and I do not retract it. **No reading is lost. All numbers are YANG's own measurements, stated with what they were measured over.

40 snapshots carry (YIN measured 50 by a narrower extraction; both agree on the property).

= 39% (header: 18 of 54 = 33%). Runners-up: variable.other 23/43, string 18/62, meta.embedded 17/23,
markup.bold 11/55, markup.italic 11/46. YANG reports one broken probe it corrected mid-measurement.

CIE76 ΔE of the theme default / below the median of six comparator grammars). CONDITIONAL: one home
for the anecdote, three gates stay.

reproduce in rank, direction and ratio — so the HARNESS's doc-comment integers are dated readings in
the present tense, the same defect as the RECORD's figures. One defect, not two.

(ablation-witness:361, darkness-witness:219, swallow-witness:107-108), three do NOT

bracket-witness imports the reader-scope module.

predicates — no second file is needed for the fault.
Distribution corrected: the 76 `READER <v> OWED` rows are 65 in darkness-ledger, 7 in
ablation-ledger, 4 in expected-divergence — all three read by stripping readers, so all 76 are handled
today. swallow-ledger carries five READER rows and zero OWED; adding OWED to any ONE of them makes it
live immediately.
CONSEQUENCE: light-cone's gate is one-sided by design — it refuses only rows filed OWED. A
`READER 5.4.1 OWED` row reads to it as RULED, moving it out of the refusable set, so the gate CANNOT
GO RED on that row. It does not disagree loudly; it goes silent. YANG promotes this to FIRST on either
list — the only latent fault that disarms a gate.

## A4 The ward's blind spot: lifting the exclusion is UNSAFE
one-implementation builds two populations; only the FINGERPRINT scan excludes `*.test.js`. Four other
checks in the same file already reach into tests, via a NAMED five-entry exemption map. The exclusion
carries its reason two lines above it: a test sits beside the instrument it collides, and holding a
test to the no-second-implementation rule would FORBID the collision the house requires.
RULING: CONDITIONAL — keep the exclusion, extend the existing named-exemption mechanism to the
fingerprint scan.

count right); a THIRD file carries a function of the same name that is a different function
(offset-based, returns an array) — a legibility hazard nothing reads. `source ./grammars.sh` is
inlined ONCE, not twice (the second file YIN named reads grammars.sh as a file, a different act).
So lifting the exclusion surfaces two real duplications — both fixable today without touching the ward.

bodies**, 3 distinct stems, largest family 89 rows (a filter or template-title value spanning a blank
line) — and that cause is stated a second time in the file's own header.

key grammar forces (one row per character position).

snap-tid + snap-meta — CONCEDE, nothing lost (2 and 1 sample files; a different invariant holds the

overreach-cut — CONDITIONAL, and the condition is CI, not the gate: `degraded-ground.test.js` runs the

reader of degraded ground. Fix the test's host resolution first, then the gate can go.

still / still-reach — DEFEND (sampled vs whole; the carrier floor seated at 0.9947; 23 of 4,403

The harvest's per-arm summary line is HABIT: the report counts what the manifest names and no file
states 49.
run_snapshots.sh + echo-test + list-test — CONCEDE all three, with a coupling: run_snapshots.sh is
referenced once more, by `.vscodeignore:16`, and the package gate checks manifest→package only, so a
stale ignore entry would go unreported. Delete both lines together.
The four stale present-tense counts — ALL FOUR CONFIRMED: theme-model's "Four gates" against 12
non-test readers (8 of them gates, 18 requirers total); tokenizer's "Twenty-two" against 26 non-test
(35 total); the doc tiddler's "Seventeen instruments" against 49 gates over 35 instruments — while the
tool's own header refuses to state a count; the corpus-ledger invariant's "Thirteen" against 20.

## Part C — YANG's verdict over YIN's 17, plus ordering
CONCEDE: 1, 2, 3 (promoted to FIRST), 4a, 5, 6, 7 (a correctness fix — two restatements say 111 where
the certified figure is 110, and one file contradicts itself 31 lines apart), 8 (and WIDEN), 9, 10,
12 (strings only), 13, 14, 15.
DEFEND / CONDITIONAL: 4b (decline as written; extend the exemption map instead), 11 (defend — the
swallow witness alone computes a coverage ceiling seated at 14 over a population of 97 regions, with
83 standing open under some cut and agreeing with the host; adding 800 upstream carriers opens twelve
more), 16 (move, never lose — and carry the reader-keyed report routing note with it, which no test
holds), 17 (verify by building a .vsix first; same missing package→needed direction as item 1).
YANG's own items YIN did not touch: the collider invariant's false green (name matched in a comment,
clause matched elsewhere; the real collider is excellent and invisible — one-line fix, strip comments
before the name match); two of the 49 gates writing tracked files so the report is not read-only;
four CI-blocking instruments outside the collider requirement, one with no test at all; nothing
collides the 39 invariants and no ruling says why; the deliberate absences (the within-construct
witness, the unarticulated fragment) and the two throwaway scouts that are the only implementation of
the continuity reading — all of which look exactly like gaps and dead code and are neither.

## THE BLIND SPOT YIN MADE VISIBLE TO YANG
The record and the harness have NO SYNTAX for "this number was true when measured" versus "this number
is true now", and every staleness finding in both reports is downstream of that one absence. Arrived at
from four directions: a ledger row stating 585/122/247 against the certified 556/110/245 while
narrating a sequence; two restatements saying 111 for 110 in welded files in shapes the weld's patterns
do not match; 106 figures of N-of-65 or a percentage in the welded section with ZERO read by anything
and only 6 machine-readable twins in the whole repository; and three harness doc-comment derivations
that reproduce in rank and ratio but not in integer.
CURE, one mark: a dated reading carries its date, a live claim carries a machine-readable twin, and a
figure carrying neither fails its gate. That single distinction retires YIN's items 7, 8 and 10 and
YANG's wave-one staleness class at once — the only item on either list that pays for itself across
both the record and the harness.

## Ordering advice
Item 3 first (the only latent fault that disarms a gate). The dated-reading mark second (retires four
items). Then 1, 2, 5, 6, 7, 10, 13, 14, 15, 4a freely. Hold 11 and 17 for measurement. Decline 4b as
written.

## Not verified
No .vsix built · no gate report, tool suite, backtrack, snapshot, canary or theme gate run (gates
actually run across both waves: the five overreach arms and divergence-staleness) · three doc-comment
integers not reproducible (claimed only as not-reproducible, not as wrong) · two OWED counting methods
differ (330/93 by line grep, 319/92 by reason-splitting; the distinct-reason counts 22 and 5 are robust
to that) · YIN's attic fixture count (7 vs 6), node:test declaration counts, copula densities and the
two sandbox probe claims unverified.

What you refuse.** Items that look obvious and are not — the reports flag deliberate absences recorded as refusals, two throwaway scouts that are the only implementation of a reading, and prose that is the only thing holding a law. Name every one you would protect from a tidy-up, and the line a future hand should read before touching it.

RESEARCH SCOUT — prior art and stated principles for three decisions a grammar repository has to make about its own test harness. Web research plus a little local reading. Report; change nothing.

═══ PRECONDITIONS (hard) ═══
- No helper agents. No Monitor watchers. Read-only: EDIT NO TRACKED FILE anywhere, commit nothing, create no worktree. Notes under `/home/joshu/.claude/jobs/86a17260/tmp/priorart/` (create it).
- You may READ `/home/joshu/Synthetic-Dream-Machine/VSCode-TW5-Syntax` (do not write there), and `/home/joshu/.claude/jobs/86a17260/tmp/fable/consolidation-plan.md` plus `/home/joshu/.claude/jobs/86a17260/tmp/trade/*.md` for context. Touch nothing in the parent repo, the bench or any container. Never `ulimit -v` on Node. Do not run gates or tests.
- Cite a source URL for every external claim. Quote the rule as the source states it; never paraphrase a normative sentence into your own words without the quote beside it.

═══ THE CONTEXT, briefly ═══
A VS Code TextMate grammar for TiddlyWiki5 plus a dialect. Its harness is 50 npm-script "gates", each printing one summary line that is HARVESTED into a wiki tiddler (`GateReport.tid`) and, for a second reader, into a JSON peer snapshot. `gate-report --check` re-runs every gate and compares its line against the harvested baseline; a mismatch reads DRIFTED. The repository already runs two readers of TiddlyWiki (a fork it develops against, and a pinned release) and keys baselines per reader.

═══ THE THREE DECISIONS ═══

**D1 — A gate whose verdict an EXTERNAL, UNPINNED tool decides.**
A new gate (`must-flag`) declares two corpus fixtures that are deliberately malformed carriers and asserts that an external CLI (`lares meme check`, built from a SIBLING repository the operator also develops) still refuses each one with its declared fault. It skips with exit 0 where that CLI is absent — so CI, which never installs it, never runs it. Today it REDS locally because the sibling repo changed its checker: the fixture is now refused for a NEW reason nobody declared. Its harvested baseline line also embeds output only producible where the CLI exists.
Research: how do projects handle a check that depends on an external tool they do not pin? Look for stated principles and real practice on — hermeticity (Bazel's hermetic-build doctrine; Nix's pure evaluation), pinning external toolchains and why, "do not test code you do not own" / testing at the contract rather than the implementation, consumer-driven contract testing (Pact et al.) and its explicit answer to "the provider changed under us", conformance suites that version their own expectations (WPT, TCKs, the CommonMark spec suite), golden/approval testing where the generator is external, and the pattern of a test that SKIPS when a dependency is absent (pytest's `importorskip`, Go's `testing.Short`/build tags, `skip` in Node's test runner) with whatever is written about when a skip is honest and when it is a lie. What do these say about a baseline file that records an optional tool's output?

**D2 — Which name is the GATE: the writer or the checker?**
The repository has pairs where one arm WRITES a derived artifact and the other arm READS and refuses on drift. Two existing pairs put the bare name on the writer and the `:check` suffix on the gate (`edition:build`/`edition:check`, `signals`/`signals:check`). A spirit just followed that precedent for two more (`ceiling` writes, `ceiling:check` gates; `builtins` writes, `builtins:check` gates). The alternative — bare name = the safe read, explicit `:write` for the mutation — was the other spirit's instinct.
Research the convention across tools that have both arms: `gofmt` / `gofmt -l` / `gofmt -w`; `prettier --check` / `--write`; `black --check` / in-place default; `rustfmt --check`; `terraform fmt -check`; `cargo fmt --check`; `clang-format -i` / `--dry-run -Werror`; snapshot test runners (`jest -u`, `UPDATE_SNAPSHOTS=1`, `cargo insta`, Python's `pytest --snapshot-update`); code generators with `-check` modes (`go generate` + `git diff --exit-code`, protobuf, `mockgen`). Two specific questions: (a) which arm do these make the DEFAULT, and what reason is given; (b) what does the literature on approval/golden testing say about making the MUTATING arm the easy one to type?

**D3 — A CI baseline that records an optional tool's output.**
The committed peer baseline for the pinned reader records a line only producible where that external CLI exists; CI never installs it, so CI's `--check` may have been reading DRIFTED on that gate since before this work. Nobody has run CI to confirm — the finding is an inference from reading the workflow.
Research: how do projects keep a recorded baseline honest when part of it is environment-dependent? Look for — conditional/optional checks in CI (`continue-on-error`, required vs optional status checks, GitHub's own guidance), partitioned baselines keyed by environment (the repository already does this per TiddlyWiki reader), recording "skipped" as a first-class result rather than omitting a line (TAP's `# SKIP` directive and its stated semantics; JUnit XML's `<skipped/>`), and anything written about a green that means "did not run".

═══ ALSO READ LOCALLY, and report what the house already believes ═══
The repository documents its own prior-art research in `docs/prior-art/*.mem` and `docs/*.mem`, and its rulings in `LEDGER-3.0.0.md`. Search those for anything bearing on these three questions — a stated principle about external readers, about which arm a name should carry, about skips, or about baselines — and quote what you find, with file and line. The house's own earlier reasoning outranks an external convention where the two differ; say where they differ.

═══ HANDBACK ═══
Per decision: the principles and practice you found, quoted with sources; where they agree and where they split; what the house already holds; and the OPTIONS each decision admits, with the cost of each — not a recommendation, an options table a reader can rule from. Then: what you did not verify, and any place where the external consensus is weaker than it looks (one loud blog post is not a convention).

  ## 2. D1 — A GATE WHOSE VERDICT AN EXTERNAL, UNPINNED TOOL DECIDES
  
  ### Hermeticity: the doctrine says an unpinned host tool is not an input at all
  
  Bazel, [Hermeticity](https://bazel.build/basics/hermeticity):
  > "When given the same input source code and product configuration, a hermetic build system always returns the same output by isolating the build from changes to the host system."
  > "Hermetic builds are insensitive to libraries and other software installed on the local or remote host machine."
  > "Hermetic build systems treat tools as source code. They download copies of tools and manage their storage and use inside managed file trees."
  > "Hermetic builds are good for troubleshooting because you know the exact conditions that produced the build."
  
  An empirical caveat worth carrying: a [2025 IEEE Software study of 70 Bazel-using OSS projects](https://mcislab.github.io/publications/2025/ieeesw-shenyu.pdf) found none had a completely hermetic build process, largely from non-hermetic top-level toolchains, with 28.57% using external tools for dependencies Bazel does not handle. So hermeticity is an **asymptote the field aims at and misses**, not a bar anyone clears.
  
  Nix's answer is the sharper one for D1: in pure evaluation mode, *reaching for the host is an error, not a fallback*. Per the [Nix reference manual, `nix eval`](https://nix.dev/manual/nix/2.18/command-ref/new-cli/nix3-eval) and surrounding issue discussion ([NixOS/nix#5825](https://github.com/NixOS/nix/issues/5825)), `builtins.getEnv` returns empty strings, `builtins.storePath` is disallowed, and `<foo>` lookup expressions throw in pure evaluation mode; `--impure` is the explicit opt-out. The transferable principle: **an environment-dependent reading should be loud at the point of reading, not silently substituted.** `must-flag`'s current skip is the silent substitution.
  
  ### "Don't test what you don't own" — real, but weaker than it is usually quoted
  
  The canonical statement is narrower than the slogan. [testdouble, *Don't mock what you don't own*](https://github.com/testdouble/contributing-tests/wiki/Don't-mock-what-you-don't-own) argues for wrapping a third-party API in your own adapter and mocking *that*. Note the verb: **mock**, not **test**. The literature's advice is the opposite of "don't test it" — [8th Light on unit-testing code boundaries](https://8thlight.com/insights/unit-testing-code-boundaries) and [the service-wrapper argument](https://naildrivin5.com/blog/2022/10/31/wrap-third-party-apis-in-service-wrappers-to-simplify-your-code.html) both say to write *integration* tests for the wrapper, precisely because a mock gives false confidence when "the library changed slightly after an upgrade." **`must-flag` IS the recommended artifact: a thin, declared contract against the real external reader.** The slogan does not condemn it. I flag this because "do not test code you do not own" was in the brief as a candidate principle, and on reading the sources it does not support retiring the gate.
  
  ### Consumer-driven contract testing has a named mechanism for exactly this situation
  
  This is the strongest external match. Pact's **pending pacts** exist for "the provider changed under us" / "an expectation nobody has declared yet."
  
  [Pact Broker — Pending Pacts](https://docs.pact.io/pact_broker/advanced_topics/pending_pacts):
  > "Enabling the 'pending pacts' feature ensures the pact verification task (and therefore, the build) only fails when a breaking change causes a previously supported pact to fail verification."
  > "When a pact version is considered 'pending', then any mismatches during verification will not cause the overall verification task to fail."
  > "Without the feature enabled, any failing pact (eg. ones with new features) will cause the provider's build to break, blocking the provider from deploying even if it is compatible with its deployed consumers."
  
  The design is a **third state between pass and fail**: a never-yet-verified expectation is *verified and reported but not blocking*, and it "graduates out of pending" once it passes, after which regression is blocking again. Mapped onto D1: the fixture's NEW undeclared fault is a pending expectation — surfaced, attributed, not blocking — until someone adjudicates it, and blocking thereafter.
  
  The complementary half, `can-i-deploy`, refuses to infer: per [Pact contract-testing writeups](https://prachub.com/resources/pact-contract-testing-interview-questions-provider-states-and-safe-deployments), where a consumer version has no verification result against the deployed provider version, the correct response is not "probably compatible because a similar version passed" — it is to obtain the missing verification or change the plan. (Secondary source; the `can-i-deploy` mechanism itself is documented at docs.pact.io, the "do not infer" phrasing is the blog's.)
  
  ### Conformance suites: the expectations travel with the thing they measure
  
  CommonMark binds spec and tests in one artifact. Per [commonmark/commonmark-spec](https://github.com/commonmark/commonmark-spec): the spec contains over 500 embedded examples that serve as conformance tests, the source is `spec.txt`, and the runner takes the spec **as an explicit argument** — `python test/spec_tests.py --spec spec.txt --program PROGRAM` ([spec_tests.py](https://github.com/commonmark/commonmark-spec/blob/master/test/spec_tests.py)). So the version of the expectations is a parameter of the run, not an ambient property of the machine. `must-flag` currently takes `lares` from `PATH` — an ambient property — and records no version of it anywhere.

  ## 3. D2 — WHICH NAME IS THE GATE: THE WRITER OR THE CHECKER?

The repo's `gate-report.js:62` SKIP regex makes the name load-bearing for routing instead — a constraint none of these tools have.

  ### (b) Approval/golden literature on making the mutating arm easy to type
  
  Here the literature is unambiguous, and it is the strongest material in this whole report.

  > "No, as of Jest 20, snapshots in Jest are not automatically written when Jest is run in a CI system without explicitly passing `--updateSnapshot`.   > "If we had any additional failing snapshot tests due to an unintentional bug, we would need to fix the bug before re-generating snapshots to avoid recording snapshots of the buggy behavior."

  > "new: write new snapshots into .snap.new files"
  > "no: does not update snapshot files at all (just runs tests)"

And the local default writes to a **sidecar** (`.snap.new`) that a separate `cargo insta accept` promotes: the write and the acceptance are different acts with different names. That is a direct structural answer to "make the mutating arm easy to type" — make the *write* easy and the *accept* explicit.

  |---|---|---|

  ## 4. D3 — A CI BASELINE THAT RECORDS AN OPTIONAL TOOL'S OUTPUT
  
  ### Partitioned baselines keyed by environment — the authoritative prior art
  
  WPT, [Test Metadata](https://web-platform-tests.org/tools/wptrunner/docs/expectation.html), names D3's two options outright:
  > "The need for different results per platform means either having multiple expectation files for each platform, or having a way to express conditional values within a certain file."
  
  and the mechanism:
  ```
  [canvas_test.html]
    expected:
      if os == "mac": FAIL
      if os == "windows" and version == "XP": FAIL
      PASS
  ```
  Conditions draw on `RunInfo` — product, os, version, debug, processor, browser_channel. Also relevant to D1's flake-vs-fault question:
  > "In the case this value is a list, the first value represents the typical expected test outcome, and subsequent values indicate known intermittent outcomes e.g. `expected: [PASS, ERROR]` would indicate a test that usually passes but has a known-flaky `ERROR` outcome."
  
  **The house already implements WPT's first option** — multiple expectation files, one per reader (`corpus/reader-signals/<version>.json`, `gate-report.js:38-44`).   insta's `INSTA_UPDATE=auto` → *"no for CI environments or new otherwise"* is the same idea applied to behaviour rather than baselines: the environment selects the arm.
  
  ### Recording "skipped" as a first-class result
  
  Both standard report formats refuse to let a skip masquerade as a pass, and both require a reason.
  
  TAP, [TAP13 specification](https://testanything.org/tap-version-13-specification.html):
  > "If the directive starts with # SKIP, the test is counted as having been skipped."
  > "The harness should report the text after # SKIP\S*\s+ as a reason for skipping."
  > example: `ok 23 # skip Insufficient flogiston pressure.`
  > whole-file form: `1..0 # Skipped: WWW::Mechanize not installed`
  
  Note the exact shape: the line **is** `ok` — the run does not fail — **and** the test is *counted as skipped*, separately, with a mandatory-in-practice reason. That is precisely the third state `must-flag` needs: exit 0, but recorded as not-run rather than as a verdict. And the whole-file example is literally "a dependency is not installed."
  
  TAP also carries a second directive the house may find closer to D1's shape:
  > "If the directive starts with # TODO, the test is counted as a todo test, and the text after TODO is the explanation."
  > "They are not expected to succeed. Should a todo test point begin succeeding, the harness should report it as a bonus."
  
  A TODO is a *known-failing, non-blocking, attributed* expectation — TAP's version of Pact's pending pact, and a candidate shape for D1-b.
  
  JUnit XML carries the same distinction structurally: a `<skipped/>` child marks a case that did not run and takes an optional `message` giving the reason, held apart from `<failure>`/`<error>`, which mean the test ran and produced an unexpected result. **Caveat: JUnit XML has no official normative schema** — it is de-facto, and every quotable description is a secondary reconstruction ([testcollab](https://testcollab.com/help/article/junit-xml-format-explained), [junitparser](https://junitparser.readthedocs.io/), [gaffer.sh](https://gaffer.sh/blog/junit-xml-format-guide/)).   GitHub's own mechanism makes this explicit, and it is the trap to avoid rather than a tool to reach for.   The repo already relies on this at `.github/workflows/test.yml:129` (`gates-host`) and line 184 — and the workflow's own comment at lines 91-95 shows the house has already reasoned about exactly this hazard:
  > "fifteen the codebase already exercises elsewhere … or under DIFFERENT terms (`signals:check`, `overreach-host`, `overreach-cut` continue-on-error in `gates-host`; `upstream-coverage` against a fresh clone in `upstream`). Running them again here, against the pinned devDependency, is not redundant in the way it looks: it makes those four checks BLOCKING for the first time, where before only their continue-on-error copies ran. That is a real strengthening of what CI enforces, not a side-effect to wave through"
  
  So the house has already ruled, in this very workflow, that a `continue-on-error` copy of a check is **not** enforcement. Any D3 option that reaches for `continue-on-error` is asking the operator to reverse that.

  | # | Option | Cost |
  |---|---|---|
  | D3-a | **Widen the baseline key to include the `lares` axis.** A second peer-file dimension (or a `lares: absent` variant), so CI compares against a baseline whose must-flag line is the skip line. | Pure extension of a mechanism the house already built and documented (`gate-report.js:38-44`), and matches WPT's "multiple expectation files for each platform". Costs a combinatorial key: readers × CLI-presence, and the key grows again at the next optional tool. |

Costs a comparison that is no longer byte-equality — and `gate-report.js:140`'s whole design is byte-equality of harvested lines. The deepest change. |

  | D3-d | **Make the gate's summary line environment-invariant.** Have must-flag print the same line either way — e.g. count declarations always (readable from `must-flag.txt` with no CLI) and report the checker reading separately. | Smallest diff; the existing harvested line `"2 declaration(s), 0 that assert nothing"` is *already* computable without the CLI.   `LEDGER-3.0.0.md:1514` — the governing precedent, and it is the *same failure mode* `must-flag` now has:
  > "The gates answer to a TiddlyWiki that always resolves. They take their verdicts from TiddlyWiki's own parser, and without one they skipped politely while the suite still reported no failures — so a contributor could break every divergence gate and read green."
  
  `LEDGER-3.0.0.md:1633`:

  `LEDGER-3.0.0.md:1595` — a skip whose *reach* nobody could predict was itself treated as the defect:
  > "Two tests resolved the TiddlyWiki this repo answers to by hand … A contributor whose checkout stood somewhere only the oracle finds saw those two skip while every other gate ran."
  
  `editions/tw5-syntax/tiddlers/CIGates.tid` — description field: *"Which gates continuous integration runs, and the reason for each one it does not"*. Its `"skipped"` array is **`[]`**. Thirteen entries sit under `notGates`, each with a `why`. **`must-flag` appears nowhere** — so the house's own record of what CI does not run says "nothing", while `must-flag` in fact runs and self-skips. `tools/gate-report.test.js:118` holds only the *gate-report SKIP pattern* to `CIGates.tid`, not runtime skips, so nothing catches this.

  `must-flag`'s own doc comment, `tools/must-flag.js:10-17`, already states the law the gate exists to enforce:

  > So the exemption carries a declaration, and the declaration gets measured: a specimen asserting a fault the checker no longer finds FAILS (the checker went blind, or the fixture went tame), and a specimen tripping a fault nobody declared FAILS too (an undeclared structure crept in beside the one the file was written to hold)."
  
  The current local RED is the **second** clause firing as designed. The gate is not broken; it is reporting. The open question is only whether a sibling-repo rewording is a *fault to adjudicate* or *noise to absorb*.
  
  ### On ledger entries that outlive their reason (the house's own answer to "the provider changed under us")
  
  `docs/differential-test-design.mem:198-209`, W5 · Ledger expiry and ownership:
  > "''Asserts:'' every ledger entry carries a reason, an owner, the probe that classified it and an expiry; a structural entry expires never, a defect entry expires and re-adjudicates.
  > ''Collision:'' an entry past its expiry fails the gate.
  > ''Must not:'' let the disagreement count fall by ledger growth. That reads identical to falling by repair and means the opposite."

  > ''Collision:'' a must-fail specimen the grammar starts reading correctly fails the gate — a positive control that passes reports a control that stopped controlling.
  > ''Ratchet:'' the known-divergence list falls; the must-fail list grows freely.
  > ''Must not:'' hold both senses in one file."
  
  `corpus/must-flag.txt` currently carries a **reason** per fault key and no **owner** or **expiry** — so by the house's own W5 it is an under-specified ledger. Note also W3's "must not hold both senses in one file": `must-flag.txt` today holds only the "written to be torn" sense; a line added for "refused for a reason nobody declared *yet*" would be the second sense, and W3 forbids fusing them.

  ## 2. D1 — A GATE WHOSE VERDICT AN EXTERNAL, UNPINNED TOOL DECIDES
  
  ### Hermeticity: the doctrine says an unpinned host tool is not an input at all
  
  Bazel, [Hermeticity](https://bazel.build/basics/hermeticity):
  > "When given the same input source code and product configuration, a hermetic build system always returns the same output by isolating the build from changes to the host system."
  > "Hermetic builds are insensitive to libraries and other software installed on the local or remote host machine."
  > "Hermetic build systems treat tools as source code. They download copies of tools and manage their storage and use inside managed file trees."
  > "Hermetic builds are good for troubleshooting because you know the exact conditions that produced the build."
  
  An empirical caveat worth carrying: a [2025 IEEE Software study of 70 Bazel-using OSS projects](https://mcislab.github.io/publications/2025/ieeesw-shenyu.pdf) found none had a completely hermetic build process, largely from non-hermetic top-level toolchains, with 28.57% using external tools for dependencies Bazel does not handle. So hermeticity is an **asymptote the field aims at and misses**, not a bar anyone clears.
  
  Nix's answer is the sharper one for D1: in pure evaluation mode, *reaching for the host is an error, not a fallback*. Per the [Nix reference manual, `nix eval`](https://nix.dev/manual/nix/2.18/command-ref/new-cli/nix3-eval) and surrounding issue discussion ([NixOS/nix#5825](https://github.com/NixOS/nix/issues/5825)), `builtins.getEnv` returns empty strings, `builtins.storePath` is disallowed, and `<foo>` lookup expressions throw in pure evaluation mode; `--impure` is the explicit opt-out. The transferable principle: **an environment-dependent reading should be loud at the point of reading, not silently substituted.** `must-flag`'s current skip is the silent substitution.
  
  ### "Don't test what you don't own" — real, but weaker than it is usually quoted
  
  The canonical statement is narrower than the slogan. [testdouble, *Don't mock what you don't own*](https://github.com/testdouble/contributing-tests/wiki/Don't-mock-what-you-don't-own) argues for wrapping a third-party API in your own adapter and mocking *that*. Note the verb: **mock**, not **test**. The literature's advice is the opposite of "don't test it" — [8th Light on unit-testing code boundaries](https://8thlight.com/insights/unit-testing-code-boundaries) and [the service-wrapper argument](https://naildrivin5.com/blog/2022/10/31/wrap-third-party-apis-in-service-wrappers-to-simplify-your-code.html) both say to write *integration* tests for the wrapper, precisely because a mock gives false confidence when "the library changed slightly after an upgrade." **`must-flag` IS the recommended artifact: a thin, declared contract against the real external reader.** The slogan does not condemn it. I flag this because "do not test code you do not own" was in the brief as a candidate principle, and on reading the sources it does not support retiring the gate.
  
  ### Consumer-driven contract testing has a named mechanism for exactly this situation
  
  This is the strongest external match. Pact's **pending pacts** exist for "the provider changed under us" / "an expectation nobody has declared yet."
  
  [Pact Broker — Pending Pacts](https://docs.pact.io/pact_broker/advanced_topics/pending_pacts):
  > "Enabling the 'pending pacts' feature ensures the pact verification task (and therefore, the build) only fails when a breaking change causes a previously supported pact to fail verification."
  > "When a pact version is considered 'pending', then any mismatches during verification will not cause the overall verification task to fail."
  > "Without the feature enabled, any failing pact (eg. ones with new features) will cause the provider's build to break, blocking the provider from deploying even if it is compatible with its deployed consumers."
  
  The design is a **third state between pass and fail**: a never-yet-verified expectation is *verified and reported but not blocking*, and it "graduates out of pending" once it passes, after which regression is blocking again. Mapped onto D1: the fixture's NEW undeclared fault is a pending expectation — surfaced, attributed, not blocking — until someone adjudicates it, and blocking thereafter.
  
  The complementary half, `can-i-deploy`, refuses to infer: per [Pact contract-testing writeups](https://prachub.com/resources/pact-contract-testing-interview-questions-provider-states-and-safe-deployments), where a consumer version has no verification result against the deployed provider version, the correct response is not "probably compatible because a similar version passed" — it is to obtain the missing verification or change the plan. (Secondary source; the `can-i-deploy` mechanism itself is documented at docs.pact.io, the "do not infer" phrasing is the blog's.)
  
  ### Conformance suites: the expectations travel with the thing they measure
  
  CommonMark binds spec and tests in one artifact. Per [commonmark/commonmark-spec](https://github.com/commonmark/commonmark-spec): the spec contains over 500 embedded examples that serve as conformance tests, the source is `spec.txt`, and the runner takes the spec **as an explicit argument** — `python test/spec_tests.py --spec spec.txt --program PROGRAM` ([spec_tests.py](https://github.com/commonmark/commonmark-spec/blob/master/test/spec_tests.py)). So the version of the expectations is a parameter of the run, not an ambient property of the machine. `must-flag` currently takes `lares` from `PATH` — an ambient property — and records no version of it anywhere.
  
  WPT goes further and makes the expectations *conditional on the configuration* (quoted in full under D3 below), with a `disabled` key whose value doubles as the reason ([Test Metadata](https://web-platform-tests.org/tools/wptrunner/docs/expectation.html)):
  > "Any values apart from the special value `@False` indicates that the (sub)test is disabled and should either not be run (for tests) or that its results should be ignored (subtests)."
  
  ### When is a skip honest?
  
  The tooling consensus is thin but consistent on one point: **a skip carries a reason, and it is counted as its own outcome.**
  
  - pytest, [`pytest.importorskip`](https://docs.pytest.org/en/stable/reference/reference.html#pytest-importorskip): *"Import and return the requested module `modname`, or skip the current test if the module cannot be imported."* Signature `importorskip(modname, minversion=None, reason=None, *, exc_type=None)` — and note `minversion`: *"If given, the imported module's `__version__` attribute must be at least this minimal version, otherwise the test is still skipped."* **The idiom has a version floor built in.** `must-flag`'s `resolveLares()` calls `lares --version` and then *discards the output* (`tools/must-flag.js:52-62`) — it uses the call only as a liveness probe. The `minversion` slot is there in the prior art and empty in the house.
  - Go, [`testing`](https://pkg.go.dev/testing): *"Short reports whether the -test.short flag is set."* · *"SkipNow marks the test as having been skipped and stops its execution…"* · the documented idiom `if testing.Short() { t.Skip("skipping test in short mode.") }` — reason string in the call.
  
  I did **not** find a canonical normative text saying "a skip that hides a missing capability is a lie." That sentence is the *house's*, at `LEDGER-3.0.0.md:1514`, and it is sharper than anything external I located. Flagging that honestly rather than dressing a blog post as a convention.
  
  ### What the prior art says about a baseline that records an optional tool's output
  
  Nothing I found endorses it. Two mechanisms exist instead, and both are in D3.
  
  ### D1 options
  
  | # | Option | Cost |
  |---|---|---|
  | D1-a | **Pin the sibling.** Record the `lares` version/commit the declaration was adjudicated against; gate reads it and refuses on mismatch. | Closest to Bazel/CommonMark doctrine and fills pytest's `minversion` slot. Requires `lares` to expose a stable version string, and couples two repos the operator moves at different speeds. Does not by itself fix CI. |
  | D1-b | **Pending-fault class (Pact's answer).** Add a third outcome: a tripped-but-undeclared fault reports and attributes, does not fail, until adjudicated; a *missing* declared fault stays blocking. | Matches the only external mechanism built for this exact problem, and preserves the half of `must-flag.js:10-17` that actually guards the fixtures. Costs a real third state in a harness whose summary lines are binary. W3 warns against fusing two senses in `must-flag.txt`, so it wants a second file or an explicit column. |
  | D1-c | **Match the contract, not the wording.** Declare the fault by a stable identifier the sibling owns (an error code), not by regex over prose. `FAULT_PATTERNS` already matches *"the reading alone, so a rewording of the construct itself … never drops a match"* (`must-flag.js:39-42`) — extend that intent one level, from construct to reading. | The contract-testing ideal, and the current red is literally a prose-rewording fault. Requires the sibling to mint stable fault codes — work in the other repo, outside this decision's reach. |
  | D1-d | **Widen the declaration to the new fault.** One-line adjudication; red goes green. | Cheapest. By W5 it is "letting the count fall by ledger growth", which *"reads identical to falling by repair and means the opposite."* Also re-arms nothing: the next rewording reds again. |
  | D1-e | **Demote to a reading.** Move `must-flag` under `CIGates.tid`'s `notGates` with a `why`, the way `edition:build` and `family-atlas` sit. | Fits an existing house category exactly, and removes it from `gate-report`'s harvest — which **also resolves D3 outright**. Costs the control: `must-flag.js:10-17`'s "a control that stopped controlling reports nothing, and reports it in green" becomes true again, which is the thing the gate was built to prevent. |
  | D1-f | **Vendor the two expected outputs as golden files**, and compare the live CLI to them only where it exists. | Makes the expectation a tree artifact, inspectable in review. Classic golden-file staleness; and the generator being external is the known-hard case for approval testing. |
  
  **Where external and house split:** the external consensus (hermeticity) says *an unpinned host tool should not decide a build's verdict at all*. The house's `LEDGER-3.0.0.md:1514` says *a gate that silently stands down is worse than one that fails*. These point opposite ways for `must-flag` — hermeticity toward D1-e, the house toward keeping it blocking and fixing the key. The house's own earlier reasoning outranks here, per the brief, and it also happens to be the position the contract-testing literature (D1-b/c) supports over the hermeticity literature.

  ## 3. D2 — WHICH NAME IS THE GATE: THE WRITER OR THE CHECKER?
  
  ### (a) Which arm is the default, and the reason given
  
  **The formatter convention splits, and this is the finding — it is not a convention.**
  
  | Tool | Default with no flag | Check arm | Source |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | `gofmt` | *"prints the reformatted sources to standard output"* — non-mutating | `-l`, `-d` | [pkg.go.dev/cmd/gofmt](https://pkg.go.dev/cmd/gofmt) |
  | `prettier` | prints to stdout; *"To format a file in-place, use `--write`."* with *"(Note: This overwrites your files!)"* | `--check` / `-c` | [prettier.io CLI](https://prettier.io/docs/en/cli.html) |
  | `clang-format` | stdout; `-i` for in-place | `--dry-run -Werror` (added after v10) | [search summary](https://github.com/rust-lang/rustfmt) — see caveat below |
  | `black` | *"Black will reformat entire files in place."* — **mutating** | `--check` (*"Don't write the files back, just return the status"*; exit 0 / 1 / 123) | [black docs, The Basics](https://black.readthedocs.io/en/stable/usage_and_configuration/the_basics.html) |
  | `rustfmt` / `cargo fmt` | in-place — **mutating** | `--check` | [rust-lang/rustfmt](https://github.com/rust-lang/rustfmt) |
  | `terraform fmt` | rewrites in place; `-write=false` *"Prevents the command from overwriting files. This behavior is implied by the `-check` flag"* — **mutating** | `-check` (*"The exit status is `0` if the command's input is properly formatted. Otherwise, the exit status is non-zero…"*) | [HashiCorp, terraform fmt](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/cli/commands/fmt) |
  
  Three non-mutating defaults, three mutating. **No convention exists on which arm is the default.**
  
  What *is* unanimous, and is the more useful finding: **in all six, the single tool name carries both arms and the CHECK is always the explicitly-flagged one.** None of them ships two differently-named entry points. The repo's *tools* already match this exactly (`--check` / `--write` on one script); the npm-script layer is a second naming system these tools simply do not have, so **the formatter precedent does not answer D2.** It answers a question the repo already settled.
  
  Two sub-findings that do transfer:
  
  1. **The default serves the person at the keyboard; CI always spells its arm out.** Every one of these projects types the longer `--check` in CI. So "which is easier to type" is a question about the *interactive* workflow, and carries no weight for gate-hood. The repo's `gate-report.js:62` SKIP regex makes the name load-bearing for routing instead — a constraint none of these tools have.
  2. **The mutating arm gets a safety net.** `gofmt -w`: *"If an error occurred during overwriting, the original file is restored from an automatic backup."*
  
  ### (b) Approval/golden literature on making the mutating arm easy to type
  
  Here the literature is unambiguous, and it is the strongest material in this whole report.
  
  [Jest — Snapshot Testing](https://jestjs.io/docs/snapshot-testing):
  > "No, as of Jest 20, snapshots in Jest are not automatically written when Jest is run in a CI system without explicitly passing `--updateSnapshot`. It is expected that all snapshots are part of the code that is run on CI and since new snapshots automatically pass, they should not pass a test run on a CI system."
  > "The goal is to make it easy to review snapshots in pull requests, and fight against the habit of regenerating snapshots when test suites fail instead of examining the root causes of their failure."
  > "If we had any additional failing snapshot tests due to an unintentional bug, we would need to fix the bug before re-generating snapshots to avoid recording snapshots of the buggy behavior."
  
  Three distinct rulings in one place: (i) writing is never the default, (ii) **a missing baseline must FAIL rather than be created**, because a freshly-written baseline passes vacuously, (iii) the explicit flag exists *as friction*, deliberately.
  
  [insta — Advanced](https://insta.rs/docs/advanced/) corroborates independently, and adds a design the house may want:
  > "auto: the default. no for CI environments or new otherwise"
  > "always: overwrites old snapshot files with new ones unasked"
  > "new: write new snapshots into .snap.new files"
  > "no: does not update snapshot files at all (just runs tests)"
  
  Note two things. The default is **environment-sensitive** — `no` in CI, `new` locally. And the local default writes to a **sidecar** (`.snap.new`) that a separate `cargo insta accept` promotes: the write and the acceptance are different acts with different names. That is a direct structural answer to "make the mutating arm easy to type" — make the *write* easy and the *accept* explicit.
  
  On the "blind approval" hazard: the clearest statement I found is in secondary material — [a 2026 approval-testing guide](https://qaskills.sh/blog/approval-testing-golden-master-guide): *"Approval testing lives or dies by diff quality. If the diff tool makes the change hard to understand, reviewers will approve blindly."* **This is one aggregator blog, not a convention.** Llewellyn Falco's primary material ([ApprovalTests](http://llewellynfalco.blogspot.com/2008/10/approval-tests.html), [SE Radio 595](https://se-radio.net/2023/12/se-radio-595-llewelyn-falco-on-approval-testing/)) is about the technique, and I did not find a normative sentence from him on this point. Jest's "fight against the habit of regenerating snapshots" is the properly-sourced version of the same claim; cite that, not the blog.
  
  ### D2 options
  
  | # | Option | Cost |
  |---|---|---|
  | D2-a | **Bare = writer, `:check` = gate.** Extend `signals`/`edition:build`/`builtins`. | Keeps three of four existing pairs. `gate-report.js:62`'s SKIP regex already excludes `signals$` and `edition`, so each new writer needs a regex entry or it is harvested as a gate — a hand-maintained list, the shape `LEDGER-3.0.0.md:1613` ("The test population derives from a walk") already condemns. Contradicts `LEDGER-3.0.0.md:1610` for `ceiling`, whose bare name mutates. Jest's "writing is never the default" lands against it. |
  | D2-b | **Bare = checker, `:write` = mutation.** Extend `snap`/`snap-update`. | Matches Jest and insta's stated reasoning, and makes `LEDGER-3.0.0.md:1610` true at the naming layer too. The SKIP regex inverts to excluding `:write` — one suffix rule, derivable, no per-name list. Costs renaming three existing scripts and any doc/CI line naming them (`edition:build` is named at workflow line 113 and `LEDGER-3.0.0.md:1561`). |
  | D2-c | **`:write` / `:check` both explicit, no bare name.** | Removes the question rather than answering it; routing becomes a pure suffix rule. Verbose at the keyboard, and the formatter precedent (one name, two flags) is against splitting at all. |
  | D2-d | **Leave the split standing**, and rule only that the SKIP regex must derive from the suffix. | Cheapest; fixes the routing fragility without touching names. Leaves the house with two conventions and the next spirit with the same coin-flip — the brief's own occasion. |
  | D2-e | **Sidecar promotion (insta's shape).** The writer writes a candidate; a named accept step promotes it. | Strongest answer to (b), and directly serves `LEDGER-3.0.0.md:1610`'s original complaint about a gate writing into a tree other tests read. Most machinery for the least immediate need. |
  
  **Where external and house split:** the formatters give no convention, so there is nothing to split from. The *snapshot* literature (Jest, insta) favours D2-b. Per the [Nix reference manual, `nix eval`](https://nix.dev/manual/nix/2.18/command-ref/new-cli/nix3-eval) and surrounding issue discussion ([NixOS/nix#5825](https://github.com/NixOS/nix/issues/5825)), `builtins.getEnv` returns empty strings, `builtins.storePath` is disallowed, and `<foo>` lookup expressions throw in pure evaluation mode; `--impure` is the explicit opt-out. The transferable principle: **an environment-dependent reading should be loud at the point of reading, not silently substituted.** `must-flag`'s current skip is the silent substitution.
  
  ### "Don't test what you don't own" — real, but weaker than it is usually quoted
  
  The canonical statement is narrower than the slogan. [testdouble, *Don't mock what you don't own*](https://github.com/testdouble/contributing-tests/wiki/Don't-mock-what-you-don't-own) argues for wrapping a third-party API in your own adapter and mocking *that*. Note the verb: **mock**, not **test**. The literature's advice is the opposite of "don't test it" — [8th Light on unit-testing code boundaries](https://8thlight.com/insights/unit-testing-code-boundaries) and [the service-wrapper argument](https://naildrivin5.com/blog/2022/10/31/wrap-third-party-apis-in-service-wrappers-to-simplify-your-code.html) both say to write *integration* tests for the wrapper, precisely because a mock gives false confidence when "the library changed slightly after an upgrade." **`must-flag` IS the recommended artifact: a thin, declared contract against the real external reader.** The slogan does not condemn it. I flag this because "do not test code you do not own" was in the brief as a candidate principle, and on reading the sources it does not support retiring the gate.
  
  ### Consumer-driven contract testing has a named mechanism for exactly this situation
  
  This is the strongest external match. Pact's **pending pacts** exist for "the provider changed under us" / "an expectation nobody has declared yet."
  
  [Pact Broker — Pending Pacts](https://docs.pact.io/pact_broker/advanced_topics/pending_pacts):
  > "Enabling the 'pending pacts' feature ensures the pact verification task (and therefore, the build) only fails when a breaking change causes a previously supported pact to fail verification."
  > "When a pact version is considered 'pending', then any mismatches during verification will not cause the overall verification task to fail."
  > "Without the feature enabled, any failing pact (eg. ones with new features) will cause the provider's build to break, blocking the provider from deploying even if it is compatible with its deployed consumers."
  
  The design is a **third state between pass and fail**: a never-yet-verified expectation is *verified and reported but not blocking*, and it "graduates out of pending" once it passes, after which regression is blocking again. Mapped onto D1: the fixture's NEW undeclared fault is a pending expectation — surfaced, attributed, not blocking — until someone adjudicates it, and blocking thereafter.
  
  The complementary half, `can-i-deploy`, refuses to infer: per [Pact contract-testing writeups](https://prachub.com/resources/pact-contract-testing-interview-questions-provider-states-and-safe-deployments), where a consumer version has no verification result against the deployed provider version, the correct response is not "probably compatible because a similar version passed" — it is to obtain the missing verification or change the plan. (Secondary source; the `can-i-deploy` mechanism itself is documented at docs.pact.io, the "do not infer" phrasing is the blog's.)
  
  ### Conformance suites: the expectations travel with the thing they measure
  
  CommonMark binds spec and tests in one artifact. Per [commonmark/commonmark-spec](https://github.com/commonmark/commonmark-spec): the spec contains over 500 embedded examples that serve as conformance tests, the source is `spec.txt`, and the runner takes the spec **as an explicit argument** — `python test/spec_tests.py --spec spec.txt --program PROGRAM` ([spec_tests.py](https://github.com/commonmark/commonmark-spec/blob/master/test/spec_tests.py)). So the version of the expectations is a parameter of the run, not an ambient property of the machine. `must-flag` currently takes `lares` from `PATH` — an ambient property — and records no version of it anywhere.
  
  WPT goes further and makes the expectations *conditional on the configuration* (quoted in full under D3 below), with a `disabled` key whose value doubles as the reason ([Test Metadata](https://web-platform-tests.org/tools/wptrunner/docs/expectation.html)):
  > "Any values apart from the special value `@False` indicates that the (sub)test is disabled and should either not be run (for tests) or that its results should be ignored (subtests)."
  
  ### When is a skip honest?
  
  The tooling consensus is thin but consistent on one point: **a skip carries a reason, and it is counted as its own outcome.**
  
  - pytest, [`pytest.importorskip`](https://docs.pytest.org/en/stable/reference/reference.html#pytest-importorskip): *"Import and return the requested module `modname`, or skip the current test if the module cannot be imported."* Signature `importorskip(modname, minversion=None, reason=None, *, exc_type=None)` — and note `minversion`: *"If given, the imported module's `__version__` attribute must be at least this minimal version, otherwise the test is still skipped."* **The idiom has a version floor built in.** `must-flag`'s `resolveLares()` calls `lares --version` and then *discards the output* (`tools/must-flag.js:52-62`) — it uses the call only as a liveness probe. The `minversion` slot is there in the prior art and empty in the house.
  - Go, [`testing`](https://pkg.go.dev/testing): *"Short reports whether the -test.short flag is set."* · *"SkipNow marks the test as having been skipped and stops its execution…"* · the documented idiom `if testing.Short() { t.Skip("skipping test in short mode.") }` — reason string in the call.
  
  I did **not** find a canonical normative text saying "a skip that hides a missing capability is a lie." That sentence is the *house's*, at `LEDGER-3.0.0.md:1514`, and it is sharper than anything external I located. Flagging that honestly rather than dressing a blog post as a convention.
  
  ### What the prior art says about a baseline that records an optional tool's output
  
  Nothing I found endorses it. Two mechanisms exist instead, and both are in D3.
  
  ### D1 options
  
  | # | Option | Cost |
  |---|---|---|
  | D1-a | **Pin the sibling.** Record the `lares` version/commit the declaration was adjudicated against; gate reads it and refuses on mismatch. | Closest to Bazel/CommonMark doctrine and fills pytest's `minversion` slot. Requires `lares` to expose a stable version string, and couples two repos the operator moves at different speeds. Does not by itself fix CI. |
  | D1-b | **Pending-fault class (Pact's answer).** Add a third outcome: a tripped-but-undeclared fault reports and attributes, does not fail, until adjudicated; a *missing* declared fault stays blocking. | Matches the only external mechanism built for this exact problem, and preserves the half of `must-flag.js:10-17` that actually guards the fixtures. Costs a real third state in a harness whose summary lines are binary. W3 warns against fusing two senses in `must-flag.txt`, so it wants a second file or an explicit column. |
  | D1-c | **Match the contract, not the wording.** Declare the fault by a stable identifier the sibling owns (an error code), not by regex over prose. `FAULT_PATTERNS` already matches *"the reading alone, so a rewording of the construct itself … never drops a match"* (`must-flag.js:39-42`) — extend that intent one level, from construct to reading. | The contract-testing ideal, and the current red is literally a prose-rewording fault. Requires the sibling to mint stable fault codes — work in the other repo, outside this decision's reach. |
  | D1-d | **Widen the declaration to the new fault.** One-line adjudication; red goes green. | Cheapest. By W5 it is "letting the count fall by ledger growth", which *"reads identical to falling by repair and means the opposite."* Also re-arms nothing: the next rewording reds again. |
  | D1-e | **Demote to a reading.** Move `must-flag` under `CIGates.tid`'s `notGates` with a `why`, the way `edition:build` and `family-atlas` sit. | Fits an existing house category exactly, and removes it from `gate-report`'s harvest — which **also resolves D3 outright**. Costs the control: `must-flag.js:10-17`'s "a control that stopped controlling reports nothing, and reports it in green" becomes true again, which is the thing the gate was built to prevent. |
  | D1-f | **Vendor the two expected outputs as golden files**, and compare the live CLI to them only where it exists. | Makes the expectation a tree artifact, inspectable in review. Classic golden-file staleness; and the generator being external is the known-hard case for approval testing. |
  
  **Where external and house split:** the external consensus (hermeticity) says *an unpinned host tool should not decide a build's verdict at all*. The house's `LEDGER-3.0.0.md:1514` says *a gate that silently stands down is worse than one that fails*. These point opposite ways for `must-flag` — hermeticity toward D1-e, the house toward keeping it blocking and fixing the key. The house's own earlier reasoning outranks here, per the brief, and it also happens to be the position the contract-testing literature (D1-b/c) supports over the hermeticity literature.
